questions.question: Explain how a hydroelectric station generates electricity, what determines its power, and set out its advantages and disadvantages including South Africa's position.
questions.expected_answer: A dam holds a reservoir; water drops through a penstock to a turbine whose runner, a wheel with curved blades or buckets, is spun by the water's weight and speed and turns a generator; the water then continues downstream, lowered but not consumed. Power depends on head, the height the water falls, and flow, the cubic metres per second, and doubling either doubles the power. Advantages are no fuel cost and no smoke, carbon dioxide, ash or waste in operation, century-long civil works, full power within a minute or two of opening a valve so it follows demand and covers peaks, about ninety percent efficiency, and water storage and flood control. Disadvantages are drowned valleys that displace people and destroy farmland, forests and river ecosystems while blocking fish and sediment, heavy evaporation in a hot climate, methane from rotting vegetation in new reservoirs, catastrophic consequences of dam failure, and dependence on rainfall so droughts cut output as at Kariba. South Africa's low erratic rainfall and small rivers limit domestic hydro to small Orange River stations at Gariep and Vanderkloof, a few percent of supply, with large hydro imported from Cahora Bassa in Mozambique over a long line that war and storms have cut.

questions.question: Describe how a pumped storage scheme works, name South Africa's three schemes with their capacities and describe Ingula, and set out the advantages and disadvantages of pumped storage.
questions.expected_answer: A pumped storage scheme has an upper and a lower reservoir joined by tunnels to a machine hall of reversible units that act as turbine-generators or motor-pumps. At night, when demand is low and coal stations must keep running, it uses their cheap surplus electricity to pump water to the upper reservoir, storing energy as height; at the evening peak it releases the water back through the same machines to generate at full power within minutes, cycling the same water daily with little lost but evaporation. South Africa has Drakensberg at 1000 megawatts, Palmiet near Grabouw at 400 megawatts and Ingula at 1332 megawatts commissioned in 2017, nearly 2700 megawatts in total; Ingula's upper Bedford dam on the Free State escarpment sits 470 metres above its lower Braamhoek dam in KwaZulu-Natal, joined by tunnels to an underground hall with four 333 megawatt reversible units, and the schemes have been vital reserves during load shedding, released in seconds when a coal unit trips. Advantages are power-station-scale storage for hours, conversion of cheap wasted night power into valuable peak power, response in seconds to minutes, clean operation and generational life, and the ability to shift midday solar surplus into the evening. Disadvantages are a net energy loss with about seventy-five to eighty percent round-trip efficiency so it pays only when night power is cheap, the need for rare sites with two reservoir locations close horizontally but hundreds of metres apart vertically with water available, enormous cost and decade-long construction as at Ingula, and the environmental footprint of dams, which at Ingula drowned wetland offset with a conservation area.

questions.question: Explain how a modern wind turbine works, set out the advantages and disadvantages of wind power in South Africa, and compare water and wind with each other and with thermal power.
questions.expected_answer: Three blades fifty to eighty metres long on a hub atop a hundred-metre tower are shaped like aircraft wings so wind flowing over them produces lift and turns the rotor at ten to twenty revolutions a minute; a gearbox or direct-drive generator in the nacelle converts the rotation to electricity; sensors yaw the nacelle into the wind and pitch the blades to catch more in light wind and less in storms; and the turbine shuts down above a cut-out speed. Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, so sites and tall towers matter. South Africa's resource is excellent along the Eastern and Western Cape coasts and parts of the Northern Cape, with some 3500 megawatts built since 2013. Advantages are free fuel with no emissions or water, the cheapest new generation alongside solar, two-year construction, land between turbines still usable for grazing and crops, and evening and night wind complementing solar. Disadvantages are variability giving about a third of rated output on average and sometimes nothing so other sources or storage are needed, visual objections, swishing noise close by, bird and bat deaths reduced by siting and shutdowns, remote sites needing transmission lines, and blades hard to recycle after twenty to twenty-five years. Water and wind both have free fuel, no operating emissions and low running costs and both depend on nature; hydro and pumped storage are flexible and controllable while wind is not; wind can be built anywhere windy while hydro needs rare sites; dams have a heavy footprint on valleys and rivers while wind farms sit lightly on land. For South Africa the combination is cheap wind and solar for bulk energy, pumped storage and batteries to shift it to the evening, flexible gas and hydro imports for gaps, and coal retiring as the mix matures.
